pages.title: Privacy
pages.content:
Privacy

This is a sample page for a fictional pub. When you ask for a table or join the House Letter, the details you send are used only to answer that request or to send that letter.

We do not sell addresses, and we keep booking emails for a few months so that we can find a table if something goes wrong. Write to tables@akane-house.example and we will remove what we hold about you.

posts.title: The Tuesday table
posts.excerpt: A knitting group has kept the window table every Tuesday afternoon since 2016.
posts.content:
Every Tuesday afternoon the same group takes the window table at Akane House. They have done it since 2016. The sitting is 15:00 to 18:00, which is walk-in, so nobody books the table in their name. They arrive after lunch has ended, while the room is still in daylight, and they stay until the staff meal at 17:30 is being laid and dinner is about to start.

The house had been open for two years when they first came. Ruth Okafor and Tomas Brandt reopened the old dye-works lodge in 2014. By 2016 the back room had become the Private Room, and the long room had a set of regulars who treated Tuesday as spoken for even though the book said otherwise. Afternoon has never taken reservations. The group fits that rule. If the window is free, it is theirs. If it is not, they take the next table along and the knitting comes out just the same.

What they order has stayed as plain as the menu. Cheese on toast with pickles and a half pint is £12, and it is the afternoon plate. Some of them take only the half. A pint of the house cask bitter, if they want a full one, is £5.40. Priya Sen is on afternoons and pastry, so the toast and the morning's bread both pass through her hands before they reach the table. Nobody in the group needs the dinner card. Two courses at £32 and three at £38 belong to the later sitting, after 18:00, when this table has usually emptied.

The window looks onto Tanner's Row. The address is 3 Tanner's Row, Eastbridge, three minutes from the Dye Works stop on tram line 2. On a Tuesday the light comes across the wood in the late afternoon and stays long enough for a chapter of a book or a few rows of knitting. People working nearby have already had the pie and gone back. Lunch, 12:00 to 15:00, is the pie of the day with mash, greens and gravy at £16, or soup, bread and butter at £9. By the time the group sits down, that service is over and the oven is no longer the centre of the room.

They are not a club we run. We do not keep a list, and we do not hold the table for fifteen minutes the way we do for a booked lunch or dinner. The fifteen-minute hold is for reservations. Tuesday afternoon has none. What they have instead is a habit the room recognises. Ruth, who is on the floor, knows the hour they tend to arrive. Ana Ferreira, who handles the book and the Private Room, does not have them in the booking notes at all. That is the point of a walk-in sitting. The table is there, the half is poured, and the chairs fill in the order people appear.

Around them the rest of the day keeps its own clock. At 08:30 the kitchen has already made bread and stock. At 11:00 the pie of the day has gone in. At 12:00 the doors opened. At 15:00 lunch ended and this quieter stretch began. At 17:30 the seven staff sit down together to eat before dinner service. The group is usually packing up as that meal starts. They are welcome to stay into the evening, but the window table on a Tuesday has always been an afternoon thing. Dinner bookings, Sunday's 12:30 and 15:00 seatings, and any private-room request go through the Book page or to tables@akane-house.example. A Tuesday knitting seat does not.

Children can be in the house until 20:00, and dogs are welcome in the bar, so the afternoon sometimes has both at nearby tables. It has never changed what happens at the window. The same bags, the same half-finished pieces, the same request for another half if the first one has gone. Last orders at 22:45 and the close at 23:00 are a long way off when they arrive. They are gone before the kitchen shuts at 21:30.

We wrote this down because the table has outlasted several menus and one change of guest cask after another. The beef and ale pie has stayed on the lunch board since 2014. The Tuesday group has stayed on the window since 2016. Neither is advertised. Both are simply still there, which is as much as a small house ought to claim.

posts.title: The pie that stayed
posts.excerpt: Beef and ale has been on the lunch menu since the first day in 2014.
posts.content:
The beef and ale pie has been on the lunch list since the first day in 2014. Everything else has changed at least once, but the pie stayed, and Ines Varga now makes it.

The pastry is crimped by hand at 08:30, and the pie goes into the oven at 11:00 so that it comes out for noon. It is served with mash, greens and gravy for £16.

posts.title: Last orders at 22:45
posts.excerpt: Why the bar stops at 22:45, and what the room does in the half hour after.
posts.content:
Last orders at Akane House are at 22:45, and the doors close at 23:00. The quarter of an hour in between is for finishing a drink without being hurried, and for the staff to start putting the room back in order.

Jonah Whitfield works the bar in the evening. He rings the bell once, polishes the last glasses, and the cellar is checked at 23:30, after everyone has gone.
